items.h: What is the opinion of the Papists concerning the prohibition of habitual lust?
items.e: They pretend that the law of God respects only the corruption of our actions, but not the habit or principle from whence they proceed.

items.h: How are they refuted?
items.e: From the spirituality of the law, which extends to the motions of the heart, as well as the actions of the life, Rom. 7:14, 23.

items.h: If, the first motions of corruption are not entertained, but immediately curbed and restrained, why are they prohibited as sinful?
items.e: Because, however soon they are curbed or restrained; yet having once been in the soul, they cannot but leave a stain and pollution behind them, contrary to the holiness and purity required in the law, James 1:14.

items.h: Who are they that are sensible of these inordinate motions and affections of the heart, and are humbled for the same?
items.e: None properly but the regenerate; as is evident from the instance of the apostle, who says of himself, after his conversion, "I had not known lust, except the law had said, Thou shalt not covet," Rom. 7:7.

items.h: What is the apostle's meaning in these words?
items.e: It is, as if he had said, I had not known this strong propensity that is in my heart to all manner of sin, even before it be consented to, or deliberately committed; unless the Spirit of God had discovered it to me, in this precept of the law forbidding the same.

items.h: How does this propensity to sin evidence itself?
items.e: In that no sooner is the object presented, than instantly there is an inordinate motion and affection of the heart after it. The combustible matter within catches fire at the very first spark of temptation, Josh. 7:21.

items.h: What may we learn from the general scope of this, and all the other commandments?
items.e: That though we could forbear the evil, and do the good contained in every commandment, it would not be sufficient, except we did it for the Lord's sake, out of love to him, and regard to his authority, Ezek. 20:19.

items.h: Is any man able perfectly to keep the commandments of God?
items.e: No mere man, since the fall, is able, in this life perfectly to keep the commandments of God, but doth daily break them, in thought, word, and deed.

items.h: What is it perfectly to keep the commandments of God?
items.e: It is, from a nature perfectly holy, to yield constant and uninterrupted obedience to them, both in heart and life, Matt. 22:37, 39.

items.h: Was ever any man, in this world, able to keep the commandments of God in this manner?
items.e: Yes; Adam, before his fall, was able to give perfect obedience to them all, Eccl. 7:29 - "God made man upright."

items.h: Whether was Adam's ability to keep the commandments of God, concreated with him, or, was it a superadded gift?
items.e: It was concreated with him, as being made after the image of God, Gen. 1:27.

items.h: Has none, since the fall, been able to keep them perfectly?
items.e: No mere man has ever been able to do it, since that time, Rom. 3:9, 10.

items.h: What do you understand by a mere man?
items.e: One who is no more than a man; and all Adam's family, descending from him by ordinary generation, are only mere men, Acts 17:26.

items.h: Why is the limitation of no mere man inserted in the answer?
items.e: That Christ might be excepted, who is infinitely more than a man, being IMMANUEL, "God with us," Matt. 1:23.

items.h: Why should HE be excepted?
items.e: Because he not only yielded perfect obedience to the law in our nature, but an obedience meritorious of life, for all his spiritual seed, Matt. 3:15; Rom. 5:17, 19.

items.h: Do not the saints, in this life, keep the commandments of God perfectly?
items.e: No; "for there is not a just man upon earth, that doeth good, and sinneth not," Eccl. 7:20.

items.h: Will they ever be capable of doing it?
items.e: Yes; when they come to heaven, where they are made perfect, Heb. 12:23; and where "the former things are passed away," Rev. 21:4.

items.h: Why are they not able perfectly to keep them in this life?
items.e: Because of the remains of corruption cleaving to every one of them, while in this world, Rom. 7:23; and from which they long to be delivered, verse 24.

items.h: But may not grace received in this life enable them to keep the commandments of God perfectly?
items.e: There is no promise of any such grace, nor would it be consistent with the gradual nature of spiritual growth, as the saints do not arrive at their full stature till they come to glory, 1 Thess. 3:13.

items.h: How does it appear from scripture, that the saints cannot attain perfection in this life?
items.e: The scripture expressly affirms, that "in many things they offend all," James 3:2; and it records the failings and infirmities of the most eminent of them that ever lived, such as Abraham, Gen. 20:2; Moses, Psalm 106:33; David, 2 Sam. 11:4, 15; Peter, Matt. 26:72, 74; and many others.

items.h: Do not the saints themselves ingenuously acknowledge, that they cannot attain perfection while here?
items.e: Yes; Job 9:20 - "If I say, I am perfect, it shall also prove me perverse." Paul, likewise, Phil. 3:12 - "Not as though I had already attained, or were already perfect."

items.h: But is it not said that Noah, Gen. 6:9; Hezekiah, Isaiah 38:3; and Job, Job 1:8, were each of them perfect?
items.e: The perfection ascribed to them, is only comparative; that is, they were more holy and circumspect than many others; but it cannot be understood of absolute perfection, as their sins and blemishes stand also upon record: Noah, for drunkenness, Gen. 9:21; Hezekiah, for ingratitude, 2 Chron. 32:25; and Job, for some degree of impatience under the rod, chap. 3.

items.h: If the saints cannot attain perfection in this life, why is it said, that they do not commit sin? 1 John 3:9 - "Whosoever is born of God, doth not commit sin."
items.e: The meaning is, they do not take pleasure and delight in sin, nor make a trade of it, as unregenerate persons do, who are therefore called "the workers of iniquity," Psalm 125:5.

items.h: Is not the perfection of sincerity attainable by the saints?
items.e: They may attain to a very high and eminent degree of sincerity in this world, Psalm 18:23; 2 Cor. 1:12; but the absolute perfection of this, or any other grace, is not to be expected by them, till they come to heaven, 1 Cor. 13:12.

items.h: Will they not be accepted upon such sincerity as they can attain to, though short of the perfection required in the law?
items.e: Their acceptance before God is not founded on their sincerity, or any other branch of their sanctification; but solely in their justification, by which the "righteousness of the law" is fulfilled in them, in virtue of the surety righteousness imputed to them, Rom. 8:4; and thus they are "accepted in the Beloved," Eph. 1:6.

items.h: Since none of mankind are able, in this life, perfectly to keep the commandments of God, how often does the answer say that they break them?
items.e: It says that they break them daily or continually, Gen. 6:5.

items.h: In what do they daily break them?
items.e: They do it in thought, word, and deed.

items.h: Is there any other possible way of breaking the commandments of God?
items.e: No; there is no other way of breaking any of them, (as to actual transgression,) than either in our thoughts, words, or deeds; and our doing so, in all these respects, shows the justice of that charge which the Lord has against every one of us, Jer. 3:5 - "Behold, thou hast spoken and done evil things as thou couldst."

items.h: How do we break the commandments of God in our THOUGHTS?
items.e: When our thoughts are sinfully employed either with reference to God, ourselves, or our neighbours.

items.h: When are our thoughts sinfully employed about God?
items.e: When they are entertaining unworthy and unbecoming notions and conceptions of him, Psalm 50:21, and 94:7, such as reflect dishonour upon his perfections and providence, Zeph. 1:12; or such as are inconsistent with the discovery he has made of himself, as being "in Christ reconciling the world to himself," 2 Cor. 5:19.

items.h: When are our thoughts sinfully exercised about ourselves?
items.e: When they are gratifying our pride, Obadiah ver. 3, ambition, Isaiah 14:13, 14, and self-applause, Rom. 12:3.

items.h: When are they sinfully employed about our neighbours?
items.e: When they are meditating and indulging envy, Gen. 4:15; reproach, Jer. 20:10; or revenge against them, Gen. 27:41.

items.h: What is the aggravating evil and malignity of sinful thoughts?
items.e: The evil and malignity of them consists in this, that they are the immediate source and spring from whence all our sinful words and deeds flow; "for out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh," Matt. 12:34.

items.h: What is the proper remedy and antidote against sinful thoughts?
items.e: The Spirit's taking the things of Christ, and showing them unto us, John 16:14, by which they will become the subject matter of our meditation and highest esteem: "for where the treasure is, there will be the heart also," Matt. 6:21.

items.h: How do men break the commandments of God by their WORDS?
items.e: When, besides idle and unprofitable words, Matt. 12:36, they utter such as are more directly dishonouring to God, Psalm 73:9, 11, and hurtful and prejudicial to themselves and others, Psalm 140:3.

items.h: How do they break them by their DEEDS?
items.e: When those sins are committed, which have been conceived in the thought, and uttered by the tongue; being inconceivably more than can be condescended upon, "for, innumerable evils have compassed us about," Psalm 40:12.

items.h: What may we learn from man's inability to keep the commandments perfectly in this life?
items.e: That we must be wholly indebted to the free grace of God, for salvation and eternal life, Titus 3:5, and not to any thing in ourselves, who are, at best, but unprofitable servants, Luke 17:10.

items.h: Are all transgressions of the law equally heinous?
items.e: Some sins in themselves, and by reason of several aggravations, are more heinous in the sight of God than others.

items.h: What do you understand by some sins being more heinous than others?
items.e: That they are more abominable, hateful, and offensive to God than others are, Ezek. 8:6, 13, 15.

items.h: Are not all sins hateful, and offensive to God?
items.e: Yes; but not equally so, Matt. 7:3 - "Why beholdest thou the MOTE that is in thy brother's eye, but considerest not the BEAM that is in thine own eye?"

items.h: How does it appear that all sins are not equally offensive to God?
items.e: From the different degrees of punishment that shall be inflicted in the other world, Matt. 11:22 - "But I say unto you, it shall be more tolerable for Tyre and Sidon in the day of judgment than for you." See also Luke 12:47, 48.

items.h: In whose sight are some sins more heinous than others?
items.e: In the sight of God, who is the best judge of the heinousness of sins, Job 36:9.

items.h: In what respects are some sins more heinous in the sight of God than others?
items.e: Some are more heinous in themselves, and some are so by reason of several aggravations.

items.h: What is it for sins to be heinous in themselves?
items.e: It is to be heinous in their own nature, though no other aggravating circumstances should attend them.

items.h: How are these sins, that are in their own nature more heinous than others, commonly ranked?
items.e: Sins committed more immediately against God, or the first table of his law, are more heinous in their own nature, than sins committed more immediately against man, or any precept of the second table. Likewise, some sins against the second table, are more heinous in themselves, than other sins against the said table.

items.h: What examples are usually given of both these?
items.e: Blasphemy against God, is more heinous in its own nature, than defaming, or speaking evil of our neighbour, 1 Sam. 2:25; and adultery is more heinous than theft, Proverbs 6:30, to the end of the chapter.

items.h: "What are those aggravations that make some sins more heinous than others?"
items.e: "Sins receive their aggravation, 1. From the persons offending. 2. From the parties offended. 3. From the nature and quality of the offence. 4. From the circumstances of time and place."102

items.h: How may the persons OFFENDING be viewed?
items.e: They may be viewed, either as to their age, gifts, or office.

items.h: What aggravation arises from the age of the persons offending?
items.e: If persons are advanced in years, by which they may be supposed to have more experience, their sins are more highly aggravated than if committed by children, or such as are raw and inexperienced, Job 32:7.

items.h: How are sins aggravated from the gifts of the persons offending?
items.e: If the offenders have been eminent for their profession, 2 Sam. 12:14, or have had a larger measure of gifts, 1 Kings 11:9, or grace, James 4:17, conferred upon them, their sins will be proportionably aggravated beyond others, who have not been so privileged.

items.h: How are sins aggravated from the office, or station, in which persons offending may be placed?
items.e: If the persons who give the offence be in an eminent station in the world, or vested with any office in the church, Jer. 23:11, 14, or in the state, 1 Kings 14:16; their sins cannot but be of a deeper tincture and dye, because their example is more likely to be followed by others, Jer. 23:14.

items.h: How do sins receive their aggravation from the parties OFFENDED?
items.e: If committed "immediately against God, his attributes and worship; against Christ and his grace; against the Holy Spirit, his witness and working; against superiors, and such as we stand especially related and engaged unto; against any of the saints, particularly weak brethren: - and the common good of all, or many."103

items.h: On what account is sin aggravated as being committed immediately against God, his attributes and worship?
items.e: In as much as it is doing evil in his sight, Psalm 51:4; is despising "the riches of his goodness," Rom. 2:4; and undervaluing his ordinances, Mal. 1:8, and the glory he has stamped upon them, verse 14.

items.h: In what consists the heinousness of sin, as being against Christ and his grace?
items.e: In its being a slighting and contemning the only remedy which infinite wisdom has provided for our malady, Acts 4:12; and surely there can be no escape, if we "neglect so great salvation," Heb. 2:3.

items.h: How is sin aggravated by its being committed against the Holy Spirit, his witness and working?
items.e: In as much as it is a rejection of his testimony without us, in the word, John 15:26, and a quenching his motions and operations within us, 1 Thess. 5:19.

items.h: What aggravation does sin receive, as being committed against superiors, and such as we stand especially related and engaged to?
items.e: In so far as sin is committed against any of these, it is a violation of the most sacred bonds, both of nature, Proverbs 30:17, and gratitude, Psalm 55:12, 13.

items.h: How is it aggravated, as being committed against the saints, particularly weak brethren?
items.e: As being committed against the saints, it is a contempt of the image of God in them, Luke 10:16; and as against weak brethren, it is laying a stumbling-block before them, by which they may be ensnared and fall, 1 Cor. 8:12.

items.h: Who are they that sin against the common good of all men, or many of them?
items.e: They are such as do what in them lies to hinder the propagation of the gospel where it is not, and to mar the success of it where it is, 1 Thess. 2:15, 16; there being nothing that tends more to the common good of all men, than the word of this salvation being sent among them, Acts 13:26.

items.h: What is the aggravation of this sin?
items.e: It makes those who are guilty of it bear the nearest resemblance they can to the devil, who aims at nothing more than the ruin and destruction of mankind, 1 Pet. 5:8.

items.h: How are sins aggravated from the NATURE and QUALITY of the offence?
items.e: They are much aggravated, "if the offence be against the express letter of the law; break many commandments; - if it break forth in words and actions; - admit of no reparation; - if against conviction of conscience; - if done deliberately obstinately, and with delight."104

items.h: Why is the offence said to be aggravated from being committed against the express letter of the law?
items.e: Because in this case there can remain no manner of doubt about the sinfulness of the action; and therefore it must be sinning with the greatest boldness and presumption, Rom. 1:32.

items.h: What aggravation is there in breaking many commandments at once?
items.e: The sin thus becomes a Complicated offence, containing many crimes in the bosom of it; like David's sin in the matter of Uriah, 2 Sam. 12:9.

items.h: How is sin aggravated by breaking forth in words and actions?
items.e: Sinful words and actions reflect a more public dishonour on God, Matt. 5:22, and do greater injury to men, Micah. 2:1, than if they were latent only in the thought.

items.h: What aggravation is there in those sins which admit of no reparation?
items.e: Their admitting of no reparation, cannot fail to aggravate them in the very nature of things; thus murder or adultery cannot but be more heinous than theft, because there may be restitution of one kind or other for theft, Lev. 6:4, 5; but nothing can compensate the taking away of the life of another, Num. 35:31 or the violation of the marriage-bed and covenant, Proverbs 6:35.

items.h: What is the aggravation of sinning, against convictions of conscience?
items.e: This kind of sinning offers violence to ourselves, contrary to the checks of that judge and reprover which every one has in his own breast, Rom. 1:32.

items.h: What is the evil of sinning deliberately, obstinately, and with delight?
items.e: It argues the giving a kind of defiance to the Almighty, Ex. 5:2; a rooted hatred of him, Rom. 8:7; and is a strong evidence of judicial blindness and hardness of heart, Zech. 7:11, 12.

items.h: What aggravation do sins receive from the circumstance of TIME?
items.e: They are more heinous if committed on the Lord's day, Jer. 17:27, or on days occasionally set apart for fasting or thanksgiving, Isaiah 22:12, 13, than at other times.

items.h: How are sins aggravated from the circumstance of the PLACE in which they are committed?
items.e: An offence is more heinous, if it be done in a land of gospel light, Isaiah 26:10; or if committed "in public, or in the presence of others, who are thereby likely to be provoked or defiled, 2 Sam. 16:22."105

items.h: What improvement should we make of this doctrine of sin in its aggravations?
items.e: To be more humbled and abased before the Lord, under a sense of our sins thus aggravated, Ezra 9:6; and likewise so much the more to admire the riches of pardoning mercy, as extended to the very chief of sinners, 1 Tim. 1:13, 15.

items.h: What doth every sin deserve?
items.e: Every sin deserves God's wrath and curse, both in this life, and that which is to come.

items.h: What do you understand by the desert or demerit of sin?
items.e: It is that in the nature of sin, which of itself deserves all that wrath and curse, which God, in his infinite justice, has entailed upon it, Gal. 3:10.

items.h: What is it in the nature of sin, which, of itself, deserves this wrath and curse?
items.e: It is the opposition, and contrariety of it to the holiness of God expressed in his law, Hab. 1:13; which is the very thing that constitutes the enormity, or heinousness of it, Jer. 44:4.

items.h: Can wrath be ascribed to God as it is a passion?
items.e: No; for all passions, properly speaking, are inconsistent with God's absolute unchangeableness, Mal. 3:6, and independency, Acts 14:15.

items.h: What then is to be understood by God's wrath?
items.e: That most pure and undisturbed act of his will, which produces most dreadful effects against the sinner, Isaiah 33:14.

items.h: What are these dreadful effects, which the wrath of God produces against the sinner?
items.e: All the miseries of this life, death itself, and the pains of hell for ever.106

items.h: Is the desert of sin separable from the nature of it?
items.e: No; as sin is the very opposite of God's holy nature and righteous law, it cannot but deserve his wrath and curse, Rom. 6:23.

items.h: If every sin deserves God's wrath and curse, must not the sins of believers deserve the same likewise?
items.e: Whatever be the desert of their sin, their persons can never be exposed, or liable to God's vindictive wrath, either in this life, or that which is to come, Zeph. 3:17; Hos. 13:14.

items.h: Why cannot the persons of believers be liable to the wrath and curse of God?
items.e: Because of their union with Christ, Rom. 8:1, who has fulfilled all righteousness for them, ver. 33, 34; or answered all the demands of law and justice in their room and stead, chap. 4:25.

items.h: What do the Papists mean by venial sins?
items.e: Such sins as are in their own nature so small and trivial, that they do not deserve eternal punishment.

items.h: Are there any sins in this sense venial?
items.e: By no means; for the least sin, being committed against a God of infinite perfection, must, on that account, be objectively infinite, and consequently deserve an infinite punishment, 2 Thess. 1:9.

items.h: May not smaller offences be atoned for, by human satisfaction or penances?
items.e: "Even the least sin - cannot be expiated, but by the blood of Christ," Heb. 9:22; 1 Pet. 1:18, 19.107

items.h: What may we learn from the desert of sin?
items.e: The amazing love of God, in transferring the guilt and punishment of sin, to the glorious Surety, making "him to be sin for us, who knew no sin, that we might be made the righteousness of God in him," 2 Cor. 5:21.

items.h: What doth God require of us that we may escape his wrath and curse, due to us for sin?
items.e: To escape the wrath and curse of God, due to us: for sin, God requireth of us faith in Jesus Christ, repentance unto life, with the diligent use of all the outward means whereby Christ communicateth to us the benefits of redemption.

items.h: What weighty argument or motive (among many others,) does the scripture afford, for essaying the practice of what God requires of us?
items.e: That though we are enjoined, to work out our own salvation with fear and trembling; yet, we are at the same time assured, that "it is God which worketh in us, both to will and to do, of his good pleasure," Phil. 2:12, 13.

items.h: Does God require any thing of us in point of duty, without promising suitable furniture, for the performance of it?
items.e: No; for he has said, "I will cause you to walk in my statutes, and ye shall keep my judgments, and do them," Ezek. 36:27.

items.h: Can we escape the wrath and curse of God, due to us for sin, by any thing we can do of ourselves?
items.e: No, surely; for "all our righteousnesses are as filthy rags," Isaiah 64:6; and, "by the works of the law, shall no flesh be justified," Gal. 2:16.

items.h: Why then does the answer say, that to escape the wrath and curse of God, due to us for sin, God requires of us, faith in Jesus Christ, repentance unto life, and a diligent use of all the outward means?
items.e: Because, though these duties, as performed by us, can neither give a title to, nor possession of eternal life; yet God appoints and requires them, both as they are MEANS of conveying and improving the salvation purchased, 1 Cor. 1:21, and likewise, as they are EVIDENCES of our interest in it, when conveyed, John 6:47.

items.h: Why does God require faith in Jesus Christ as the sovereign means of escaping his wrath and curse?
items.e: Because there is salvation in no other; there being "none other name under heaven, given among men, whereby we must be saved," Acts 4:12.

items.h: What encouragement have we to essay believing in Jesus Christ?
items.e: There cannot be a greater encouragement than this, that faith "is the gift of God," Eph; 2:8; and accordingly the promise runs, "I will say, It is my people, and they shall say, The Lord is my God," Zech. 13:9.

items.h: Why is repentance unto life required?
items.e: Because it is the inseparable fruit and effect of faith or believing, Zech. 12:10 - "They shall look upon me whom they have pierced, and they shall mourn for him."

items.h: What encouragement have sinners of mankind, privileged with gospel light, to look for, or expect this blessing of repentance unto life, which God requires of them?
items.e: They are warranted to expect it on this ground, that as Christ has "received gifts for men," Psalm 68:18, so "him hath God exalted with his right hand to be a Prince and a Saviour, to give repentance to Israel," Acts 5:31.

items.h: Why does God require of us the diligent use of all the outward means whereby Christ communicates to us the benefits of redemption?
items.e: Because a neglect or contempt of the means of divine appointment, for communicating the benefits of redemption, is, in the sight of God, the same thing as a neglect or contempt of these inestimable benefits themselves, Luke 10:16 - "He that despiseth you, despiseth me; and he that despiseth me, despiseth him that sent me."

items.h: Can our believing, repenting, and diligent use of means, as they are acts of ours, be the procuring cause of our escaping wrath, or found our title to life and salvation?
items.e: No; for, "by the deeds of the law, there shall no flesh be justified in his sight," Rom. 3:20. Our security from wrath and title to heaven, are founded on the imputation of the surety righteousness alone, Isaiah 45:25.

items.h: What would be the consequence of making our faith, repentance, and good works, the procuring cause of our escaping the wrath and curse of God due to us for sin?
items.e: This would be setting aside the satisfaction of Christ, and making a saviour of our duties, than which nothing could nail us more effectually down under the curse, Gal. 3:10 - "As many as are of the works of the law, are under the curse."

items.h: Have unbelieving and impenitent sinners any warrant to conclude, that they have escaped the wrath and curse of God, due to them for sin?
items.e: No, surely; for "he that believeth not, is condemned already," John 3:18; and our Lord says, "Except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish," Luke 13:3.

items.h: Is our escaping the wrath and curse of God suspended on the condition of our faith, repentance, and diligent use of the outward means?
items.e: No; for, if any promised blessing were suspended upon the condition of our personal obedience, it would be the very form of the covenant of works, Rom. 10:5 - "Moses describeth the righteousness which is of the law, that the man which doth these things, shall live by them."

items.h: When do carnal and unregenerate men turn the dispensation of the covenant of grace into the form of the covenant of works?
items.e: When they separate the duties of faith, repentance, and the diligent use of the means, from the promises of the Covenant, and hope to make themselves accepted with God by their personal performance of these duties, Rom. 10:3.

items.h: What CONNEXION have faith, repentance, and the use of outward means, with salvation?
items.e: They have the connexion of APPOINTED MEANS prescribed by God himself, which, by his blessing, are subservient for such a valuable end; being themselves a part of salvation, and evidences of it, 2 Thess. 2:13.

items.h: How are the means of salvation usually distinguished?
items.e: Into internal and external.

items.h: What are the internal means?
items.e: Faith and repentance, with the other graces that accompany or flow from them.

items.h: Why called internal, or inward?
items.e: Because they are wrought in the hearts of the elect, by the Spirit of God, as the fruits and effects of Christ's purchase and mediation, Zech. 12:10.

items.h: What are the external or outward means?
items.e: They are the ordinances of Divine institution, and appointment; such as, the word, sacraments, and prayer.

items.h: How is faith in Jesus Christ connected with salvation?
items.e: As it is the hand that receives Christ and his righteousness, as the all of our salvation, Psalm 68:31; John. 1:12.

items.h: How is repentance unto life connected with salvation?
items.e: As it consists in that godly sorrow for sin, flowing from faith, which is both the exercise and ornament (in some measure) of all the travellers Zion-ward, while in this world, Jer. 50:4; 2 Cor. 7:11.

items.h: How is the diligent use of outward means connected with salvation?
items.e: As it is by them that Christ communicates to us the benefits of redemption, Proverbs 2:1-16.

items.h: Could he not communicate the benefits of redemption, without the outward means?
items.e: Whatever he could do, yet his ordinary method is to honour his own ordinances, as the means of communicating these benefits to us, which we are not to expect but in the use of them, Proverbs 8:34; Rom. 10:17.

items.h: What USE does God require us to make of the outward means?
items.e: He requires us to make a diligent use of them.

items.h: What is a diligent use of the outward means?
items.e: It is an embracing every opportunity offered in providence, for attending upon God in them, looking earnestly for his blessing upon them, by which alone they become efficacious for our spiritual benefit, 1 Cor. 3:6, 7.

items.h: What is faith in Jesus Christ?
items.e: Faith in Jesus Christ is a saving grace, whereby we receive and rest upon him alone for salvation, as he is offered to us in the gospel.

items.h: What are the several kinds of faith mentioned in scripture?
items.e: They are these four: historical, temporary, the faith of miracles, and saving faith.

items.h: What is historical faith?
items.e: It is a bare assent to the truth of what is revealed in the word, without any real affection or regard to the things revealed in it. Such a faith as this may be found in devils, James 2:19; and in wicked men, Acts 8:13.

items.h: Why called historical?
items.e: Not merely because it believes only the histories of the Bible; but because it assents to the truths revealed in it, as being little or no way concerned in them, or without any particular application of them to the soul, Acts 28:26.

items.h: What is temporary faith?
items.e: It is such as, together with an assent to the truth of divine revelation, is also accompanied with some slight and transient motion upon the affections; which may endure for awhile, and then vanishes, Matt. 13:20, 21.

items.h: Has this kind of faith any influence upon the practice?
items.e: It may be, for a time, accompanied with an external reformation from some grosser sins, 2 Pet. 2:20.

items.h: What is the faith of miracles?
items.e: It is that peculiar gift, by which a person believes, that, by the power of God, something shall be effected by him which is quite above the power of all natural causes, 1 Cor. 13:2.

items.h: On what occasion has God bestowed upon any this faith?
items.e: For the confirmation of some extraordinary mission, or of some important article of revealed religion; as the miracles of Moses under the Old Testament; and of the apostles under the New.

items.h: Was not the faith of miracles, in the days of our Saviour and his apostles, conferred upon some who were not in a state of salvation?
items.e: Yes; both the extraordinary gift of the faith of miracles, and the ordinary and common gifts of the Spirit, were conferred upon some, who, we are assured, will be utterly rejected of God, Matt. 7:22, 23 - "Many will say unto me in that day, Lord, Lord, have we not PROPHESIED in thy name? and in thy name have CAST OUT DEVILS? and in thy name done many WONDERFUL WORKS? And then will I profess unto them, I never KNEW you: depart from me, ye that work iniquity."

items.h: What is saving and justifying faith?
items.e: It is that faith in Jesus Christ, which is described in the answer, "whereby we receive and rest upon him alone for salvation," &c.

items.h: Why is this faith, described in the answer, called a grace?
items.e: Because it is the gift of God, freely bestowed upon the sinner, Eph. 2:8, who has no antecedent worth, value, or good qualification, of which he can boast, 1 Cor. 4:7.

items.h: Why a saving grace?
items.e: Because wherever true faith is, there salvation is already begun, which shall certainly be consummated in due time, John 3:36.

items.h: Where is the connexion established between faith and salvation?
items.e: Faith being the gifted hand that is stretched out to receive Christ in the promise, Psalm 68:31, cannot but be inseparably connected with salvation; because Christ, whom faith receives, is the ALL of our salvation, Col. 3:11: hence is that promise, Mark 16:16 - "He that believeth - shall be saved."

items.h: Why is it called faith in Jesus Christ?
items.e: Because Christ is the main, or principal object of saving faith, Acts 16:31.

items.h: Why do you call him the main or principal object of faith?
items.e: Because nothing can fill the eye or hand of faith, but Christ only, or God in him, Psalm 73:25.

items.h: How is faith in Jesus Christ denominated in the answer?
items.e: It is called a receiving, John 1:12, and resting on him, Psalm 37:7.

items.h: Are there not other denominations of faith in Christ of the same divine authority with those mentioned?
items.e: Yes; such as eating, drinking, flying, entering, and many others.

items.h: From whence are these various denominations of faith derived?
items.e: From the different views in which Christ is represented in the word.

items.h: How may the above denominations of faith be applied to the different views in which Christ is represented in the word?
items.e: When the flesh and blood of Christ (or his incarnation and satisfaction) are exhibited as meat indeed, and drink indeed; faith, in conformity to this, is called eating and drinking of the same, John 6:55, 56; when Christ is held forth as a refuge, faith is a flying to him for safety, Heb. 6:18; and when he is represented as a door, faith is an entering in by him, John 10:9.

items.h: Why is faith, in the answer, expressed by receiving?
items.e: Because Christ, the glorious object of it, is revealed in scripture, under the notion of a gift, 2 Cor; 9:15, presented to such as are quite poor, and have nothing of their own, Rev. 3:17, 18.

items.h: Can there be a receiving of Christ, without a previous giving of him?
items.e: No; there may indeed be a giving, where there is no receiving, because the gift may be refused; but there can be no such thing as a receiving of Christ, without a giving of him before; for "a man can receive nothing except it be given him from heaven," John 3:27.

items.h: Why is faith called a resting on Christ?
items.e: Because he is revealed in the word as a firm foundation, Isaiah 28:16, on which we may lay the weight of our everlasting concerns, with the greatest confidence and satisfaction, Psalm 116:7.

items.h: To what other scripture expression is resting on Christ equivalent?
items.e: It is the same with TRUSTING in him, Isaiah 26:4; or relying on his righteousness and fulness, as laid out in the word, for our unanswerable plea, and inexhaustible treasure, chap. 45:24.

items.h: For what end do we receive Christ and rest upon him?
items.e: For salvation, Acts 15:11.

items.h: What is the salvation for which we receive and rest upon Christ?
items.e: It is salvation from sin, Matt. 1:21, as well as from wrath, 1 Thess. 1:10; consisting in a life of holiness here, as well as of happiness hereafter. It is salvation begun in this life, and consummated in glory, Rev. 3:21.

items.h: Why are we said to receive and rest upon Christ alone for this salvation?
items.e: To exclude every thing else except Christ himself, and his righteousness, as the ground of our confidence before God, and title to eternal life, Acts 4:12.

items.h: What else do men ordinarily rest upon for salvation?
items.e: Upon the general mercy of God; the works of the law; or a mixture of their own works with the righteousness of Christ.

items.h: Who are they that rest on the general mercy of God?
items.e: They who never saw the necessity of a satisfaction to law and justice, in order to the honourable exercise of mercy, according to Ex. 34:7.

items.h: Who are they who rest on the works of the law, as the ground of their confidence?
items.e: Such as have never been convinced that the demands of the law are utterly above their reach, Gal. 3:12.

items.h: Who are they that are for blending or mixing their own works with the righteousness of Christ, as the ground of their hope?
items.e: Such as foolishly imagine they can supply what is defective in their own obedience, by what Christ has done for them, Rom. 9:31, 32.

items.h: To what does our Lord resemble this practice?
items.e: To the putting "a piece of new cloth into an old garment," by which "the rent is made worse," Matt. 9:16.

items.h: Are not the very expressions of receiving and resting on Christ, designed to exclude the works of the law, from being any part of the ground of our hope of salvation?
items.e: Yes; for, when a poor man receives his alms, or a weary man sits down, and rests himself; neither of them can, in any propriety of speech, be said to work.

items.h: Upon what warrant do we receive and rest upon him for salvation?
items.e: Upon the warrant of his being offered.

items.h: To whom is he offered?
items.e: He is offered to us, men and women of Adam's family, in contradistinction to the angels that fell, Heb. 2:16.

items.h: Where is the offer made?
items.e: In the gospel.

items.h: What is the gospel as containing this offer.
items.e: It is good tidings, Luke 2:10; or the promise of eternal life, 1 John 2:25, to sinners of mankind, as such, through Jesus Christ our Lord, Proverbs 8:4.

items.h: Though the offer of Christ to us be last mentioned, in the answer, yet is it not the first thing to Be believed?
items.e: Surely it is; for unless one believe that Christ is offered to him as a Saviour, he will never receive and rest upon him for salvation, Rom. 10:14.

items.h: Who offers Christ to us in the gospel?
items.e: God, essentially considered in the person of the Father, makes the original or authentic gospel offer of him, John 6:32 - "My Father GIVETH you the true bread from heaven."

items.h: In what form or tenor does this authentic offer run?
items.e: In the form of a deed of gift, or grant, in which he makes over his Son, Jesus Christ, to mankind lost, that whosoever of them all shall receive this gift, shall not perish, but have eternal life.

items.h: In what text of scripture (amongst others) is this grant, or authentic gospel offer, contained?
items.e: It is expressed in so many words, John 3:16 - "God so loved the world, that he GAVE his only begotten Son, that WHOSOEVER believeth on him should not perish, but have everlasting life."

items.h: Who are they that offer Christ to sinners in subordination to God?
items.e: Ministers of the gospel, who have a commission from him so to do, 2 Cor. 5:19, 20.

items.h: What is the ministerial offer?
items.e: It is the publishing or proclaiming of Heaven's gift, or grant, to sinners of mankind, without exception, as the foundation of their faith or warrant to believe, 1 John 5:11.

items.h: What would be the consequence, if there were any exception in the authentic gospel offer?
items.e: The consequence would be, that no ministerial offer of Christ could be made to the party excepted, more than to the fallen angels.

items.h: Does the universality of Heaven's grant, and of the ministerial offer founded on it, infer a universal redemption as to purchase?
items.e: By no means; it only infers a universal warrant to believe.

items.h: How do you prove that it infers a universal warrant to believe?
items.e: From this, that if there were not such a gift and grant of Christ as warranted all to receive him, the unbelieving world could not be condemned for rejecting him, as we find they are, John 3:18 - "He that believeth not is condemned already."

items.h: Is there any analogy, or proportion, between our receiving and resting on Christ, and the offer that is made of him in the gospel?
items.e: Yes; we receive and rest upon him as he is offered in it, 1 Cor. 15:11 - "So we preach, and so ye believed."

items.h: How is he offered in the gospel?
items.e: He is offered freely, wholly, and particularly.

items.h: How do you prove, that he is offered, and should be received freely?
items.e: From Isaiah 55:1 - "Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters, and he that hath no money; come ye buy and eat; yea, come, buy wine and milk, without money and without price;" Rev. 22:17 - "Whosoever will, let him take the water of life FREELY."

items.h: Why is Christ to be received freely?
items.e: Because God, out of his sovereign and matchless love, makes a free gift of him to mankind sinners, John 3:16, as being infinitely above all price, Job 28:13-24.

items.h: What do the proud and legal hearts of sinners bring as a price for Christ, who is absolutely inestimable?
items.e: Their duties, their good qualifications, their honest aims, their sincere endeavours, and the like.

items.h: Why do they presume to bring such things as these?
items.e: Because they know not that they are "wretched, and miserable, and poor, and blind, and naked," Rev. 3:17.

items.h: What is it to receive Christ wholly?
items.e: It is to receive him in his person, as vested with all his relative offices, of prophet, priest, and king.

items.h: Why must he be received wholly?
items.e: Because there is nothing of Christ we can possibly do without: standing in absolute need of him, as a prophet for instruction; as a priest, for righteousness; and as a king, for sanctification, 1 Cor. 1:30.

items.h: What is it for a person to receive Christ particularly?
items.e: It is to be verily persuaded that Christ is his, upon the grant and offer of him, in the word, to him in particular, John 7:37, and 9:36.

items.h: Is it not sufficient that a man believe, that the grant and offer of Christ is to sinners of mankind in general?
items.e: No; there can be no benefit by a belief of the general offer, without a particular application, or appropriation of it to the person himself, 1 Tim. 1:15.

items.h: How is this illustrated by an example?
items.e: It is commonly illustrated thus: If a king makes a proclamation of pardon and indemnity to all the rebels within his kingdom, it is plain, that every individual rebel must either believe the pardon of his own crime of rebellion in particular, or else reject the king's proclamation of grace, and continue in his rebellious practices: there is no medium.

items.h: Is not believing that an indemnity is offered to rebels in general, a medium between the two?
items.e: No; because loyal subjects, who need no pardon, may believe that a general indemnity is offered to rebels; and this even rebels themselves may believe, who yet may reject the benefit of that indemnity, and continue in their rebellion, John 5:40.

items.h: Is a belief and persuasion of the mercy of God in Christ, and of Christ's ability and willingness to save all that come to him, all that is necessary to constitute justifying faith?
items.e: No; because there being no appropriation, or particular application in this persuasion, it can be no more than such a faith as devils and reprobates may have; or such as Papists and Arminians may subscribe to, consistently with their other errors and heresies.

items.h: What is that appropriating persuasion, in the nature of faith, which is necessary to answer the call and offer of the gospel?
items.e: It is not a persuasion that Christ is mine in possession, or that I am already in a state of grace: but a persuasion that Christ is mine in the gift of God, and offer of the gospel, Zech. 13:9 - "I will say, It is my people; and they shall say, The Lord is my God": and therefore I appropriate to myself the common salvation, Acts 15:11; or what did lie before me in common, in the gospel offer, I take home to my own soul in particular, Gal. 2:20 - "Who loved me, and gave himself for me"believing that I shall have life and salvation by Christ; and that whatever he did, for the redemption of sinners, he did it for me.

items.h: Why is an appropriating persuasion (or, a man's being persuaded that Christ is his in particular) necessary to the nature of saving and justifying faith?
items.e: Because nothing can relieve the sinner from the curse of the law, accusing and condemning him in particular, but faith's application of an offered Saviour, as "made a curse" for him in particular, to deliver him from that 'law-curse,' Gal. 3:10, 13.

items.h: How do you prove, that a particular application of Christ is the effectual relief from the curse of the law, denounced against the sinner in particular?
items.e: From this, that the free gift is as full to justification, as the offence, through the law, was to condemnation; for, "as by the offence of one, judgment came upon all men to condemnation; even so, by the righteousness of one, the free gift came upon all men to justification of life," Rom. 5:18.

items.h: Since an appropriating persuasion is necessary to the nature of faith, has every one that has true faith, always an assurance of his being in a gracious state?
items.e: No; for though a believer be persuaded that Christ is his in the promise and offer of the gospel: yet, through the prevalency of remaining corruption, he may frequently doubt of his being in a state of grace, or of his present title to eternal life, Isaiah 49:14.

items.h: Is doubting, then, in the nature of faith, because it is incident to the believer?
items.e: Doubting can no more be said to be in the nature of faith because, through the prevalence of unbelief and corruption, it sometimes takes place in the believer, than darkness can be said to be in the nature of the sun, because it is sometimes eclipsed; for faith and doubting are, in their own nature, opposite, Matt. 21:21 - "If ye have faith, and doubt not."

items.h: Have all true believers the same measure of saving faith?
items.e: No; some are but "of little faith," Matt. 14:31; whereas others are "strong in faith; giving glory to God," Rom. 4:20. Howbeit the lowest measure of true and saving faith is infallibly connected with glory, Matt. 12:20.

items.h: What are the evidences of a strong faith?
items.e: Trusting to the bare word of a faithful and powerful God, even when the outward course of providence seems to run against the performance of the promise, Rom. 4:19; a fixed resolution to wait on the Lord, for the promised good which we want, even after seeming repulses and refusals, Matt. 15:22-29; and a sedate reposing ourselves on an unchangeable God, under all the vicissitudes of time, Psalm 112:7.

items.h: How may the weakness of faith be discerned?
items.e: The more easily a person can suspect the love and favour of God, Isaiah 40:27; the more impatient under delays of answering requests, chap. 38:14; and the more addicted to a life of sense, John 20:25, the weaker is the faith.

items.h: How may the truth and reality of saving faith be known, though it be in the weakest and lowest degree?
items.e: If we bear an inward enmity to all sins, because offensive to God, Psalm 51:4; if we can say, that it is the desire of our souls to love Christ above all things, John 21:17; and to be eternal debtors to free grace, reigning through his righteousness, Rom. 5:20, 21; then we may warrantably conclude, that our faith, however weak, is yet of a saving nature.

items.h: To what is true faith opposed in scripture?
items.e: It is opposed to a staggering at the promise, Rom. 4:20; to wavering, James 1:6; to doubting, Matt. 21:21; and, in a word, to unbelief, Mark 9:24.

items.h: Who are they who will not be charged with the sin of unbelief?
items.e: The Heathen world, who are not privileged with the light of gospel-revelation, Rom. 10:14 - "How shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard?"

items.h: What is the evil of this sin in those who are favoured with gospel light?
items.e: It makes God a liar, 1 John 5:10; treads "under foot the Son of God;" and does "despite unto the Spirit of grace," Heb. 10:29.

items.h: What is the proper seat of faith?
items.e: The HEART "for with the HEART man believeth unto righteousness," Rom. 10:10; though faith be radically in the understanding, yet it operates upon the will, which embraces the object with particular application, Heb. 11:13.

items.h: Is knowledge necessary to saving faith?
items.e: It is so necessary that there can be no saving faith without it, 1 John 4:16 - "We have KNOWN and believed the love that God hath to us."

items.h: What is the difference between the knowledge of faith, and speculative knowledge?
items.e: The knowledge of faith is humbling, 1 Cor. 8:2; transforming, Acts 26:18; affectionate, 1 John 4:8; and progressive, Hos. 6:3; whereas, common or speculative knowledge has none of these properties, nor effects.

items.h: In what consists the harmony or agreement between faith, love and hopes?
items.e: By faith, we get a sight of an unseen good, and believe it, Heb. 11:27; by love we desire and seek after it, Isaiah 26:8; and by hope, we confidently expect, and patiently wait for it, Rom. 8:25.

items.h: How does faith view and consider its objects?
items.e: It views them, as certain, suitable, and invisible.

items.h: Why does it view them as certain?
items.e: Because of the unquestionable veracity of God who reveals them, John 6:69 - "We believe, and are SURE, that thou art that Christ, the Son of the living God."

items.h: Why does it consider them as suitable?
items.e: Because they are exactly adapted to the state and circumstance of the soul, whatever they are, 1 Cor. 1:30; 1 Tim. 1:15.

items.h: Why does faith view its objects as invisibles?
items.e: Because it acts and goes forth toward them, upon the bare testimony of God; not only without the concurrence of sense and carnal reason, John 20:29, but oftentimes contrary to them, Rom. 4:18, 19.

items.h: Is faith any part of our justifying righteousness?
items.e: No; we acknowledge no other righteousness, for pardon and acceptance, but the righteousness of Christ alone, Phil, 3:9.

items.h: Why then are we said to be "justified by faith"? Rom. 5:1.
items.e: Because it is faith which lays hold upon, and receives that righteousness by which we are justified, Rom 3:22.

items.h: Is not faith necessary to interest us in Christ, and the benefits of his purchase?
items.e: Yes; for though the endorsement of the promise to us, gives us a right of access, Acts 2:39; yet it is faith, that gives the right of possession, John 6:47 - "He that believeth on me HATH everlasting life."

items.h: What is repentance unto life?
items.e: Repentance unto life is a saving grace, whereby a sinner, out of a true sense of his sin, and apprehension of the mercy of God in Christ, doth, with grief and hatred of his sin, turn from it unto God, with full purpose of, and endeavour after, new obedience.

items.h: Why is the repentance, described in the answer called repentance unto life? Acts 11:18.
items.e: Because being a saving grace, it is inseparably connected with salvation, of which it is a part; and likewise to distinguish it from the "sorrow of the world," which "worketh death," 2 Cor. 7:10.

items.h: What is meant by the sorrow of the world working death?
items.e: The meaning is, that the legal sorrow, or horror of conscience, which the men of the world may have, from a dread of God, as a vindictive judge, ready to pour out the vials of his wrath and vengeance upon them, without any conception or belief of his mercy through Christ, is nothing else but the beginning of eternal death, and inconceivable misery; as was the case with Cain, Judas, and others.

items.h: Whether is repentance a transient action or an abiding principle?
items.e: It is an abiding principle, continually disposing the person to mourn for sin, and to turn from it all the days of his life, Isaiah 38:14, 15.

items.h: Is repentance then to be considered as a thing that is over with the first days of one's religion?
items.e: No; but it is to be viewed as a permanent grace, an habitual frame of soul, inclining those who are privileged with it, to mourn daily for sin, till "God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes," in heaven, Rev. 21:4.

items.h: Who is the proper subject of repentance?
items.e: None but a sinner can be the subject capable of it: for just or righteous persons "need no repentance," Luke 15:7.

items.h: By whom is it wrought in the heart of a sinner?
items.e: "By the Spirit of God," Zech. 12:10."108

items.h: What is the instrument or means, by which the Spirit works this grace?
items.e: "The word of God," Acts, 11:18, 20, 21."109

items.h: What is the instrumentality of the word, in the hand of the Spirit, for working repentance?
items.e: In the word there is a display of the holiness of the divine nature and law, to which we ought to be conformed, Lev. 19:2; the word also discovers the necessity of union with Christ, and the imputation of his righteousness, as the foundation of true holiness, 1 Cor. 1:30; together with the inevitable ruin of all who go on in their trespasses, Psalm 68:21, and all these powerfully set home, by the Spirit, upon the conscience of the sinner.

items.h: In what consists a true sense of sin?110
items.e: In a "sight and sense, not only of the danger, but also of the filthiness and odiousness of sin, Ezek. 36:31,"111 as contrary to the holiness of God, and, consequently, as highly offensive to him, Psalm 51:4.

items.h: How is a true sense of sin begotten in the soul?
items.e: By faith, or an apprehension of the mercy of God in Christ.

items.h: May there not be a sense of sin without this apprehension of the mercy of God in Christ?
items.e: Yes; but not a true sense; there may be a sense of sin as hurtful to the person, Gen. 4:13; but not as hateful to God, Hab. 1:13.

items.h: Why is the mercy of God said to be apprehended in Christ?
items.e: Because though God is essentially merciful, yet his mercy can have no egress towards any sinner of mankind, consistent with the honour of his justice and holiness, except through the obedience and satisfaction of Christ, Ex. 34:6, 7.

items.h: What is it to APPREHEND the mercy of God in Christ?
items.e: It is the same with faith, or believing; it being by faith only, that we can lay hold upon his mercy, Psalm 13:5.

items.h: Is it from faith then that repentance flows, as the proper source of it?
items.e: Yes; for though faith and repentance are graces given together, and at once in respect of time; yet, in the order of nature, the acting of faith goes before the exercise of repentance, Zech. 12:10.

items.h: How does it appear, from scripture, that faith goes before repentance, in the order of nature?
items.e: The scriptures set forth the blessed object of faith, and the promises of rich grace, as powerful motives and inducements to repentance, Jer. 3:14; Joel 2:13; by which it is evident that it must be by a believing application of this glorious object, brought nigh in the promise, that a sinner is enabled to exercise true repentance, Acts 11:21 - "And a great number believed, and turned unto the Lord."

items.h: How may the precedency of faith be evinced from the nature of repentance itself?
items.e: Repentance is turning from sin unto God; but there can be no turning to God, but through Christ, John 14:6; and no coming to Christ except by faith, chap. 6:35.

items.h: Is not repentance placed before faith in scripture, Mark 1:15 - "Repent ye, and believe the gospel"?
items.e: The reason is, repentance being the end, and faith the means to that end; though the end be first in one's intention, yet the means are first in practice. Thus, in the text quoted, Christ commands sinners to repent; but then in order to their repenting, he commands them to believe the gospel, as the only way to do it.

items.h: How are we sure, that where repentance is named before faith in scripture, it is to be understood of repentance as the end, and of faith as the only way and means?
items.e: From Acts 20:21:"Testifying - repentance toward God, and faith toward our Lord Jesus Christ" where it is obvious, that if "faith toward our Lord Jesus Christ" is not the "means of repentance toward God," that fundamental truth would be destroyed, that "Christ is the only way to the Father," as he himself affirms, John 14:6 - "No man cometh unto the Father but by me."

items.h: Is repentance to be separated from faith?
items.e: No; though these graces are to be distinguished, yet they are never to be separated from one another; being conjoined in the same promise, Zech. 12:10 - "They shall LOOK upon me whom they have pierced, and they shall MOURN for him."

items.h: What is the evil of maintaining that none but true penitents have a warrant to embrace Christ by faith?
items.e: It sets sinners upon spinning repentance out of their own bowels, that they may fetch it with them, as a price in their hand to Christ, instead of coming to him by faith, to obtain it from him, as his gift, Acts 5:31.

items.h: What are the constituent parts, or ingredients, of true repentance, as flowing from faith?
items.e: Grief and hatred of sin; turning from it unto God; with full purpose of, and endeavour after, new obedience.

items.h: What is that grief which is an ingredient of true repentance?
items.e: It is a real, inward and abiding sorrow for sin, as offensive and dishonouring to a holy and gracious God, Job 40:4, 5.

items.h: What is that hatred of sin, which accompanies true repentance?
items.e: It is not only a loathing and abhorring of our sin, but of ourselves, on account of it, Isaiah 6:5.

items.h: What are the qualities of this hatred?
items.e: It is universal, against all sin, Psalm 119:104; and irreconcilable to any known sin, Psalm 101:3.

items.h: What is the formal nature of evangelical repentance, or that which properly completes it?
items.e: It is when a sinner doth, with grief and hatred of his sin, turn from it unto God.

items.h: From what does the sinner turn in repentance?
items.e: He turns from sin; because a continuance in the practice of sin is inconsistent with repentance, Ezek. 14:6 - "Repent and turn - from your idols, and turn away your faces from all your abominations."

items.h: How can penitents be said to turn from sin, when it remains in them, and they are daily offending while in this life?
items.e: Though they cannot shake themselves loose of the being and remains of sin, yet they turn from it, not only in their life and conversation, but likewise in their heart and affection.

items.h: How do they evidence that they turn from it in their life and conversation?
items.e: By resisting the outbreakings of sin, and all temptations to it, Psalm 18:23; by watching against all occasions of it, Proverbs 4:14, 15; and endeavouring to "have always a conscience void of offence toward God, and toward men," Acts 24:16.

items.h: How do they manifest their turning from sin in heart and affection?
items.e: In as much as though sin cleaves to them, they do not cleave to it, as formerly, but hate and loathe it, Psalm 119:104, 113.

items.h: To what does the sinner turn in repentance?
items.e: He turns unto God, Hos. 6:1 - "Come, and let us return unto the Lord."

items.h: Do not many turn from one sin to another, and never to God?
items.e: Yes; "They return, but not to the Most High," Hos. 7:16.

items.h: What is the true cause of the sinner's turning to God?
items.e: It is his being turned unto God first, Jer. 31:19 - "Surely, after that I was turned, I repented."

items.h: How is the sinner turned unto God first?
items.e: By the Spirit's working faith in him, whereby he receives and rests on Christ for salvation, of which remission of sin, and repentance, are a part, Acts 5:31.

items.h: In what does the sinner's turning to God consist?
items.e: It consists in his turning to the loving of God, as his Lord and Master, Isaiah 26:13; and to his duty to him as such, Acts 9:6.

items.h: How does the returning sinner express his love to God, as his Lord and Master?
items.e: By a voluntary choice of him as his only Lord, Hos. 2:7; and by looking upon his service as the greatest freedom and happiness, Psalm 84:4.

items.h: How does he testify his returning to his duty to God, as his Lord and Master?
items.e: By a full purpose of, and endeavour after new obedience.

items.h: What is the nature of this purpose of duty to God, into which the true penitent enters?
items.e: It is a purpose or resolution to return to the practice of every known duty, Psalm 119:106, and to spirituality in it, Phil. 3:3.

items.h: Why called a FULL purpose?
items.e: Because it is not only a resolution of what a person will do hereafter, but a resolution which is immediately put in execution, without delay, Psalm 119:60 - "I made haste, and delayed not to keep thy commandments;" like the prodigal, who says, "I will arise, and go to my father;" and immediately he arose and went, Luke 15:18, 20.

items.h: What is the inseparable concomitant of this full purpose in all true penitents?
items.e: An endeavour after new obedience.

items.h: Why is a full purpose of new obedience connected with an endeavour after it?
items.e: Because purposes, without endeavours, are but like blossoms without fruit, which can never prove one to be a true penitent, Matt. 21:30.

items.h: Why called an endeavour after new obedience?
items.e: Because, though the penitent is sensible he cannot perform this kind of obedience in his own strength, yet he aims at it, and at no less than perfection in it, Phil. 3:14 - "I press toward the mark, for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus."

items.h: Why is the obedience which the true penitent purposes and endeavours after, called new obedience?
items.e: Because it is such an obedience as flows from a new principle, is influenced by new motives, performed in a new manner, and is aimed at a new end.

items.h: What is the new principle from which this obedience flows?
items.e: A principle of faith, Rom. 14:23, and a principle of love, John 14:15.

items.h: What are the new motives by which this new obedience is influenced?
items.e: The "grace of God," Titus 2:11, 12; and the "love of Christ," 2 Cor. 5:14, 15.

items.h: What are the motives by which men, in a natural state, are influenced to duties?
items.e: The dictates of a natural conscience, Rom. 2:15; their own interest and reputation, Matt. 6:5, a mercenary hope of heaven, Micah 6:6, 7, or a slavish fear of hell, Isaiah 33:14.

items.h: What is the new manner in which new obedience is performed?
items.e: It is performed in the strength of Christ, Phil. 4:13; or in a dependence on the furniture secured in the promise, 2 Cor. 12:9; it is done with delight, Isaiah 64:5; and with the whole heart, Psalm 119:69.

items.h: What is the new end at which it aims?
items.e: The glory of God is the ultimate end of it, 1 Cor. 10:31.

items.h: What is the difference between legal and gospel repentance?
items.e: Legal repentance flows from a dread of God's wrath, Matt. 27:3-6; but gospel repentance from the faith of his mercy, Psalm 130:4; in legal repentance, the sinner is taken up mostly with the fatal consequences of sin, Isaiah 49:9-12; in gospel repentance, he is chiefly affected with the evil nature of it, as contrary to the holy nature and law of God, Luke 15:21.

items.h: What are the motives that should produce repentance?
items.e: The command of God, Acts 17:30; the suffering of Christ, Zech. 12:10; and the certain danger of impenitency, Luke 13:5.

items.h: What are the evidences of true repentance?
items.e: The very same that are mentioned by the apostle, 2 Cor. 7:11 - "For behold, the self-same thing that ye sorrowed after a godly sort, what carefulness it wrought in you; yea, what clearing of yourselves; yea, what indignation; yea, what fear; yea, what vehement desire; yea, what zeal; yea, what revenge?

items.h: What is that carefulness which is a mark of the true penitent?
items.e: It is carefulness about the one thing needful, that good part which shall not be taken away, Luke 10:42.

items.h: Upon what ground will the true penitent clear himself?
items.e: Only upon the ground of the surety-righteousness imputed to him, Isaiah 45:24.

items.h: What is the principal object of his indignation?
items.e: It is sin, as striking immediately against God, Psalm 51:4, compared with Psalm 119:104.

items.h: What is that fear, which is an evidence of true repentance?
items.e: It is a filial and reverential fear of God, or a standing in awe to offend him, Gen. 39:9.

items.h: What is that vehement desire, with which a true penitent is privileged?
items.e: It is an earnest and ardent desire after conformity to God, and fellowship with him, Psalm 27:4.

items.h: What kind of zeal is it, that is evidential of gospel repentance?
items.e: It is zeal for the glory of God, and the interest of Christ in the world, Psalm 137:5, 6.

items.h: What is that revenge, which is competent to a true penitent?
items.e: It is Such a revenge against sin, as aims at its utter ruin and extirpation, Rom. 7:24.

items.h: In what respects is repentance necessary?
items.e: It is necessary in respect of the command of God, Acts 17:30, and as evidential of the reality of faith, of which it is the native fruit, and effect, Zech. 12:10.

items.h: May not this duty be delayed or put off for a while?
items.e: No; because of the uncertainty of time, Luke 12:19, 20, and of the continuance of the Spirit's striving, Gen. 6:3.

items.h: When should the Lord's people apply to him, for the exercise of this grace of repentance, in a more especial and particular manner?
items.e: After great falls, 2 Sam 12:13; when under severe trials, or deep affliction, 2 Sam. 15:26, 30; and when they are to ask of God some singular favour or mercy, Dan. 9:8, compared with verses 18, 19.

items.h: By what means may the lively exercise of repentance be attained?
items.e: By looking on it as the gift of Christ, Acts 5:31; and by viewing our sins as laid on him, who was pierced for them, Zech 12:10; together with searching and trying our ways, Lam. 3:40.

items.h: What are the outward and ordinary means whereby Christ communicateth to us the benefits of redemption?
items.e: The outward and ordinary means whereby Christ communicateth to us the benefits of redemption, are his Ordinances, especially the word, sacraments, and prayer, all which are made effectual to the elect for salvation.

items.h: What do you understand by the benefits of redemption?
items.e: All the blessings of Christ's purchase, which may be summed up in grace here, and glory hereafter, Psalm 84:11.

items.h: Who communicateth these benefits or blessings to us?
items.e: Christ himself, who has them wholly at his disposal, Luke 22:29 - "I appoint unto you a kingdom."

items.h: How comes Christ to have the disposal of them wholly in his hands?
items.e: By his Father's gift, John 3:35 - "The Father loveth the Son, and hath GIVEN all things into his hand;" and by his own purchase of them; hence called a "purchased possession," Eph. 1:14.

items.h: What is it for Christ to communicate the benefits of redemption?
items.e: It is not to give away the property of them from himself, but to make us "sharers with him" in them all; that is, to make us "heirs of God, and joint heirs with Christ," Rom. 8:17.

items.h: Does Christ communicate them in a mediate or immediate way?
items.e: In a mediate way, through the intervention of ordinances, Eph. 4:11-14.

items.h: What are the ordinances by which Christ communicates to us the benefits of redemption?
items.e: They are "prayer and thanksgiving, in the name of Christ; the reading, preaching, and hearing of the word; the administering, and receiving the sacraments; church government and discipline; the ministry and maintenance thereof; religious fasting; swearing by the name of God, and vowing unto him."112

items.h: Why are these called His ordinances?
items.e: Because they are all of them instituted and prescribed by him in his word, as the alone King and Head of his church, to be observed in it to the end of the world, Matt. 28:20.

items.h: Have we any reason to expect, that the benefits of redemption will be communicated by ordinances of man's invention and appointment?
items.e: No; for all such ordinances, having no higher sanction than the commandments of men, are declared to be IN VAIN, Matt. 15:9; they are condemned as will-worship, Col. 2:23; and the observers of them severely threatened, Micah. 6:16.

items.h: Why is it said, especially the word, sacraments, and prayer?
items.e: Because, though the other ordinances above mentioned are not to be excluded, as being all of them useful in their own place; yet the word, sacraments, and prayer, are the chief or principal outward means for communicating the benefits of redemption, Acts 2:42.

items.h: What is the special usefulness of the word for communicating the benefits of redemption?
items.e: In the word these benefits are exhibited and offered to sinners of mankind, as the ground of their faith, that, believing they may be possessed of them all, John 20:31.

items.h: What is the special usefulness of the sacraments for communicating these benefits?
items.e: The sacraments represent to our senses, 1 Cor. 10:16, what the word does to our faith, and are designed for the confirmation of it, Rom. 4:11.

items.h: What is the special usefulness of prayer for the above purpose?
items.e: The prayer of faith fetches home to the soul all the good that is wrapped up both in the word and in the sacraments, Mark 11:24 - "What things soever ye desire when ye pray, believe that ye receive them, and ye shall have them."

items.h: Why are the word, sacraments, and prayer, called means, by which Christ communicates to us the benefits of redemption?
items.e: Because he is pleased to begin and carry on the work of grace in the soul, by and under these ordinances, Acts 2:41, 42.

items.h: Why called the outward means?
items.e: To distinguish them from faith, repentance, and other inward means; and particularly to distinguish them from the inward and powerful influences of the Holy Spirit, which are necessary to accompany the outward means in order to salvation, Zech. 4:6.

items.h: Why called ordinary means?
items.e: Because they are the stated and ordinary way and method, by which Christ communicates the benefits of redemption to sinners of mankind, Rom. 10:14-18; Ezek, 37:28.

items.h: Are there any extraordinary means without the word, by which Christ communicates the benefits of redemption to adult persons?
items.e: No; for whatever providences God may make use of, when he is beginning or carrying on his work of grace in the soul, Acts 9:3-7; yet these dispensations are always to be considered in a subserviency to the word, chap. 16:25-33, or as occasions of the Spirit's working in concurrence with it, 2 Pet. 1:18, 19.

items.h: Are the ordinances, of themselves, effectual for communicating the benefits of redemption?
items.e: No; they are made effectual, Rom. 1:16.

items.h: To whom are they made effectual?
items.e: To the elect only, Acts 13:48.

items.h: For what end are they made effectual to the elect?
items.e: For salvation, Heb. 10:39

items.h: What is meant by salvation?
items.e: Not only a begun deliverance from all sin and misery, and a begun possession of all happiness and blessedness in this life, John 3:15; but likewise a total freedom from the one, and a full and uninterrupted enjoyment of the other, in the life to come, Rev. 21:4.

items.h: If the ordinances are made effectual to the elect only for salvation, why have others, in the visible church, the benefit of them?
items.e: To show the infinite intrinsic sufficiency of the satisfaction of Christ, 1 John 4:14; and, at the same time, to render those who slight such valuable privileges the more inexcusable, John 15:22.

items.h: What may we learn from Christ's instituting his Ordinances to be the outward and ordinary means of salvation?
items.e: We may from thence learn the difference between the church militant, which sees but through a glass darkly, and the church triumphant, which sees "face to face," 1 Cor. 13:12

items.h: How is the word made effectual to salvation?
items.e: The Spirit of God maketh the reading, but especially the preaching of the word, an effectual means of convincing and converting sinners, and of building them up in holiness and comfort, through faith, unto salvation.

items.h: What is meant by the word in this answer?
items.e: The whole of divine revelation, contained in the scriptures of the Old and New Testament.

items.h: What has God appointed with reference to his word, that it may be effectual to salvation?
items.e: He has appointed the reading, John 5:39; "but especially the preaching thereof," 2 Tim. 4:2.

items.h: "Is the word of God to be read by all?"
items.e: "Although all are not permitted to read the word publicly to the congregation, Deut. 31:9, 11, yet all sorts of people are bound to read it apart by themselves, chap. 17:19, and with their families, chap. 6:7."113

items.h: What is the meaning of these words in our Larger Catechism, "all are not permitted to read the word publicly to the congregation?"
items.e: The meaning is: not, as if there were an order of men appointed by Christ, to be READERS in the church, distinct from ministers; but only, that none ought to read publicly to the congregation, except those whose office it is, not only to read the word of God, but to explain it to the edification of others, Neh. 8:8 - "So they read in the book of the law of God distinctly, and gave the SENSE, and caused them (namely, the people) to understand the reading."

items.h: Why is the reading of the scriptures apart by ourselves necessary for every one?
items.e: Because the scriptures are a sword for defence, Eph. 6:17; a lamp for direction, Psalm 119:105; and food for nourishment, Jer. 15:16; in all which respects they are necessary for every Christian travelling Zion-ward, 2 Tim. 3:16, 17.

items.h: May not the reading of the scriptures in our families, supersede the reading of them apart by ourselves?
items.e: No; the doing of the one ought by no means to jostle out the other.

items.h: What is essentially requisite in order to capacitate the unlearned to read the scriptures?
items.e: That they be "translated out of the original into vulgar languages, 1 Cor. 14:11."114

items.h: How is the word of God to be read?
items.e: "The holy scriptures are to be read with a high and reverend esteem of them, Neh. 8:5; with a firm persuasion that they are the very word of God, 2 Pet. 1:21; and that he only can enable us to understand them, Luke 24:45."116

items.h: Why should we read the scriptures with a high and reverend esteem of 115them?
items.e: Because they are dictated by the Holy Ghost, and "are able to make us wise unto salvation," 2 Tim. 3:15.

items.h: Why should we read them with a firm persuasion that they are the very word of God?
items.e: Because without this we can never build our hope on them, as containing the words of eternal life, 1 Thess. 2:13.

items.h: Why should we read them with a persuasion that God only can enable us to understand them?
items.e: Because, without this, we cannot exercise a dependence upon him, for that spiritual and internal illumination, which is necessary to a saving and experimental knowledge of them, 1 Cor. 2:10.

items.h: "By whom is the word of God to be preached?"
items.e: "Only by such as are sufficiently gifted, Mal. 2:7, and also duly approved and called to that office, Rom. 10:15; 1 Tim. 4:14."116

items.h: Who are they that are sufficiently gifted?
items.e: They are such as are not only of a blameless moral walk, and "have a good report of them that are without," 1 Tim. 3:7; but likewise such as have a competent stock of human literature, Titus 1:9; and are, in the judgment of charity, reputed to be pious and religious men, 2 Tim. 1:5.

items.h: What is it to be duly approved and called to that office?
items.e: It is not only to be approved by the presbytery, who have the sole power of trying the ministerial qualifications, and of ordination to that office, 1 Tim. 4:14; but likewise to have the call and consent of the people, who are to be under the pastoral inspection and charge, Acts 1:23, and 14:23.

items.h: "How is the word of God to be preached by those that are called thereunto?"
items.e: They are to preach sound doctrine "diligently, plainly, faithfully, wisely, zealously, and sincerely."117

items.h: What are we to understand by sound doctrine?
items.e: The whole system of divine truth, contained in the holy scriptures, or evidently deducible from it; particularly whatever has the greatest tendency to depreciate self, and to exalt Christ, who ought to be the main and leading subject of all gospelpreaching, 2 Cor. 4:5.

items.h: What is it to preach sound doctrine diligently?
items.e: It is to be instant "in season, and out of season," 2 Tim. 4:2118 embracing every opportunity of doing good to souls; and watching for them, "as they that must give account," Heb. 13:17.

items.h: What is it to preach plainly?
items.e: It is to essay it, "not in enticing words of man's wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit, and of power," 1 Cor. 2:4.119

items.h: What is it to preach the word faithfully?
items.e: It is a "making known the whole counsel of God," (or at least a not shunning to do so), Acts 20:27.120

items.h: When may ministers be said to preach wisely?
items.e: When in studying, or preaching, they are wholly taken up in applying themselves to the necessities and capacities of the hearers,"121 Luke 12:42; 1 Cor. 3:2.

items.h: When do they preach the word zealously?
items.e: When they do it "with fervent love to God, and the souls of his people,"122 2 Cor. 5:14, and 12:15.

items.h: How is the word preached sincerely?
items.e: When there is an "aiming at God's glory," and his people's "conversion, edification, and salvation, 1 Thess. 2:4; 1 Cor. 9:22; 1 Tim. 4:16."123

items.h: Who is it that makes the reading and preaching of the word effectual to salvation?
items.e: (THE SPIRIT OF GOD), 1 Cor. 2:11 - "The things of God knoweth no man, but the SPIRIT of God."

items.h: How does he make them effectual?
items.e: By accompanying them with his divine power upon the soul, Rom. 1:16.

items.h: Of what is it that the Spirit of God makes the reading and preaching of the word an effectual means?
items.e: He makes them an effectual means of convincing and converting sinners, and of building them up in holiness and comfort, through faith, unto Salvation.

items.h: Does the Spirit make more frequent and ordinary use of the reading, or of the preaching of the word, for these valuable ends?
items.e: He makes more frequent and ordinary use of the preaching of the word; and therefore there is an ESPECIALLY prefixed to it in the answer.

items.h: How do you prove, that the preaching of the word is honoured as the most ordinary means?
items.e: From express scripture testimony to this purpose, Acts 4:4 - "Many of them which heard the word believed;" chap. 11:20, 21 - "And some of them - spake unto the Grecians, preaching the Lord Jesus. And the hand of the Lord was with them: and a great number believed, and turned unto the Lord."124
